skills.name: Narrative writing: choices, viewpoint and consequence

note.text: A narrative develops events through a viewpoint. A complication motivates action; choices and consequences make the sequence more than a timetable. Select details contributing to action or meaning. Keep a clear time frame, with tense changes justified by relationships. Dialogue should reveal a concern or advance the event. A resolution shows change without necessarily solving every future problem. The original model is not prescribed literature.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to draft a coherent narrative in which choices produce an intelligible development. Builds on: prose, creative scene and retelling. Leads to: sentence variety and editing.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Lower Sixth extension: distinguish telling events in order from developing a narrative. Establish whose experience guides the reader, introduce a meaningful complication and show a choice with a consequence. A flashback may be useful if time relations remain clear. Do not add an unrelated rescue merely to end the piece. The original model and paper task below extend the Form Five narrative foundation; produce a new situation rather than copying its wording.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify the audience, purpose and required content. Plan the order, draft in your own words and check each feature against the model. Explain why an edit improves the answer.

paper_task.prompt: Write a narrative where an unconfirmed detail causes difficulty. Maintain viewpoint, develop a choice and consequence, and end with resolution or reflection. Include dialogue only where relevant.
model: I reached the reading room carrying the notice I had copied that morning. Visitors were gathering, but the door was locked. I looked at my handwriting and feared I had ruined the event.

“Who confirmed this room?” Manka asked. I started to say everyone had mentioned it. Then I remembered the coordinator’s words: the room was still a suggestion. I had turned a possibility into an instruction. Instead of blaming the caretaker, I admitted the mistake and asked Manka to help find the teacher.

The teacher arranged an available supervised space while we explained the change. The beginning was delayed, and some visitors had to leave. We could not undo that inconvenience. Afterwards I corrected the notice and marked the new arrangement clearly.
When I folded the old sheet away, it no longer looked like a small copying mistake. Repeating a detail confidently was different from checking it.
checklist: Narrative viewpoint: the perspective presenting events.
Complication: a problem motivating consequential action.
Causal development: events linked through choices and consequences.
Resolution and reflection: an ending showing change and significance.
Use relevant original details and check sentence boundaries, agreement and spelling.
